newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: WEST AUSTRALIAN FARMERS SOW WHEAT SECESSION CRISIS.
newsitem.headline: WEST AUSTRALIAN FARMERS SOW WHEAT SECESSION CRISIS.

text.p: A long-simmering row in Australia's A$4 billion a year wheat export sector has come to a head with a decision by Western Australian growers to split from the industry in the rest of the country.

The Western Australian Farmers Federation's (WAFF) grains council had decided to recommend the federation withdraw from the peak national grains grower body, the Grains Council of Australia (GCA), the WAFF said in a statement.

The decision followed an almost unanimous vote by Western Australian growers that they were not adequately represented at a national level by the current structure of GCA, WAFF grains section president Chris Moffet said.

"Western Australia grows approximately 43 percent of the total Australian wheat crop, which includes over 60 percent of (Australia's) export wheat, and yet has the same voting power on the GCA as states that grow only five to 10 percent," he said.

The decision, expected to be endorsed by a WAFF executive meeting on August 20, follows disagreement between Western Australian wheat growers and the rest of the industry over share issue terms in the privatised Australian Wheat Board (AWB).
As part of the dispute, WAFF has called for the AWB's 'single desk' monopoly on Australian wheat exports to be split between west coast and east coast wheat.

Grains leaders contacted by Reuters on Wednesday for their assessment of how serious the threatened split might be for the industry saw the pillars of the sector remaining intact, even if this required intervention by the Federal government.
They also said the AWB's 'single desk' monopoly on wheat exports, which they believe allows it to win on export markets, was not expected to be demolished if WAFF withdrew from the GCA.
But all see a real prospect of a Western Australian split.
Kevin McMenemy, general president of WAFF, told Reuters it would be surprising if the WAFF did not endorse its own grains council on the recommendation that it withdraw from the GCA.
The GCA will hold an emergency meeting with Australia's Minister for Primary Industries John Anderson on Monday to discuss the Western Australian split threat and other matters.
John Lush, acting GCA president, told Reuters that if the growers split it was possible the government would impose a structure for the privatised AWB on the industry.
The government was likely to follow the mainstream preferred structure for the AWB, but the industry would prefer that government adopt proposals than impose structures, he said.
Withdrawal by Western Australia would simply mean the state's growers would not have national representation. "It's just cutting off your nose to spite your face," he said.
Xavier Martin, chairman of the New South Wales Farmers' Association grains committee, told Reuters he was still optimistic that agreement could be reached on the AWB structure.
"We've seen before in the history of this federated democracy ... some states carry on with this sort of petulant and vexatious attitude to issues," he said.
Martin described the Western Australian proposal that the AWB single desk be split as "nonsense".
"I don't know whether they think they're Siamese twins or what, it's just a joke. They're obviously out (for) their own interests and to hell with the rest of the nation," he said.

The row has been triggered by the AWB's privatisation moves, which centre on the proposal that it issue A shares with full voting rights to wheat growers and B shares with restricted voting rights, for trading in a probable listing of the privatised AWB on the Australian Stock Exchange.
One demand of Western Australian growers is that A shares be issued in proportion with wheat tonnages produced by growers.
-- Michael Byrnes Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
